newsitem.title: USA: Democrats unveil plans for health coverage for kids.
newsitem.headline: Democrats unveil plans for health coverage for kids.

text.p: Senate Democrats on Thursday unveiled plans to expand health coverage to more than 10 million uninsured American children, either through vouchers or tax credits for lower- and middle-income families.

The proposals, which would cost from $3 billion to $9 billion a year, would guarantee health insurance to children up to age 18 in families that make too much money to qualify for Medicaid, but too little to buy insurance in the market.
President Bill Clinton is also expected to propose an expansion of health care for children as part of a budget plan he will submit to Congress early next month.
"Something is wrong in America when (inmates) in prison can get health care coverage, but millions of American kids can't," Iowa Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin told a news conference.

While Democrats said they were confident a political consensus was building for their plan, it was far from clear whether the Republican-led Congress, intent on balancing the budget, would approve such expensive, open-ended plans.

Congress last year approved a law making it easier for people to keep insurance if they changed jobs or had a pre-existing health condition, but that proposal had bipartisan support from its inception.

Republicans have not endorsed the Democratic proposals, but say they support the concept of expanding insurance for children. They are looking for alternatives that would rely more on the private sector and less on the government.

The White House wants to expand outreach under the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled. A recent study found that about 3 million children who are eligible for Medicaid health benefits are not enrolled in the programme.
The administration is also considering other steps as part of a $750-million-a-year initiative, congressional aides said.
Democrats have not settled on a final plan, but outlined two separate proposals on Thursday.
The first, sponsored by Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle would provide a refundable tax credit to families with incomes up to $75,000 a year to help them buy insurance.

Families with incomes up to 200 percent of the poverty line would get a refundable credit to cover 90 percent of insurance premiums. The credit would decrease on a sliding scale and phase out for families earning more than $75,000.
Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, estimated that his proposal would cost between $3 billion and $4 billion a year. It would be paid for mainly by scaling back tax breaks to big business.
The second plan, by Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy would provide vouchers for families to buy insurance.

Families earning up to 185 percent of the poverty line, which would be $24,000 a year for a family of three, would get vouchers equal to the full amount of insurance premiums. The subsidy would be phased out for families earning up to $39,000.

States would administer the plan, which, like Daschle's, includes a comprehensive benefits package. The Kennedy plan would cost an estimated $9 billion a year when fully phased in, to be paid for by a 75-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax.

The number of uninsured children in the United States has climbed to an estimated 10.5 million. The vast majority live in families with a working parent. Uninsured children are more likely to use emergency rooms and other expensive health care.
